Contar o que aconteceu e já terminou («a: Narrate what happened and is already finished («ayer», «anoche», «el año pasado») with the regular -ar, -er and -ir forms of the pretérito indefinido, get the accent marks right («hablé», «habló»), handle the spelling changes («busqué», «llegué», «empecé», «leyó»), and tell the indefinido apart from the pretérito perfecto.
Você conta, no passado, o que fez e o qu: You can now narrate, in the past, what you did and what other people did at a time that's already over. Next lesson: the pretérito indefinido of irregular verbs (fui, hice, dije, tuve, estuve…).
Você chega ao A2 já sabendo se apresenta: You're arriving at A2 already able to introduce yourself, talk about your family, order at a café, tell the time, ask for directions, narrate your routine, say what you like, and say what you've done today with the pretérito perfecto. At this level you start telling stories: what happened yesterday, last week, on vacation. The first tense you need is the pretérito indefinido, the tense for finished facts. English's simple past («I talked», «she talked») never changes shape for person, so this is genuinely new ground: Spanish has six distinct endings, and it's worth paying close attention to both the endings themselves and the accent marks that tell subjects apart.
PASSO 1: use o pretérito indefinido para: STEP 1: use the pretérito indefinido for something that happened and ended at a moment you can name: «ayer», «anoche», «el lunes», «en 2019», «hace dos días». STEP 2: for -ar verbs, drop the «-ar» from the infinitive and add these endings: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. «Hablar» becomes «hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron». STEP 3: the first person (yo) and the third person (él, ella, usted) carry a written accent: «hablé» and «habló». The accent marks the stressed syllable and also keeps the past apart from the present: «hablo» (I speak) versus «habló» (he/she spoke). STEP 4: in «nosotros», the indefinido of -ar verbs looks exactly like the present: «hablamos». Context settles it: «Ayer hablamos» is past, «Hablamos cada día» is a habit. STEP 5: «vosotros» (Spain) ends in «-asteis»: «hablasteis». In Latin America, «ustedes» uses «hablaron». STEP 6: the subject pronoun is almost always dropped, because the ending already says who it is: «Ayer cené en casa» (I had dinner at home yesterday). STEP 7: the indefinido has no connection to the present — the fact is closed off in the past. With «hoy», «esta semana» or «este año», which haven't ended yet, Spain prefers the pretérito perfecto from lesson 17: «Hoy he trabajado mucho». In much of Latin America people say «Hoy trabajé mucho» instead, since there the indefinido often takes over the perfecto's job.
as terminações lembram o pretérito perfe: English's simple past («I talked», «you talked», «he talked») never changes shape for the subject at all, so the whole idea of six distinct person-endings is new ground, not something to carry over. The trickiest traps here are specific to Spanish spelling: the «-ó» ending (with no English equivalent at all), the «-aron» plural ending, and the «vosotros» form «hablasteis», which has no counterpart in English either since English marks no distinction between «you» singular and «you» plural. The written accent is another new habit: English never marks stress with an accent mark, but in Spanish it's what tells «hablo» (I speak, present) apart from «habló» (he/she spoke, past).
Last year I traveled to Valencia.
Last night we had dinner at Marta's place.

PASSO 1: os verbos em -er e em -ir usam: STEP 1: -er and -ir verbs use the same endings in the indefinido: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. «Comer» becomes «comí, comiste, comió, comimos, comisteis, comieron». «Vivir» becomes «viví, viviste, vivió, vivimos, vivisteis, vivieron». STEP 2: the first person «-í» and the third person «-ió» carry an accent: «comí», «comió». STEP 3: in «nosotros», -ir verbs look just like the present («vivimos»), but -er verbs change: present «comemos», indefinido «comimos». STEP 4: watch the third-person ending closely: it's «comió», «vivió» — never anything resembling an English-style reduction. And the plural is «comieron», never «comeron». STEP 5: to keep the sound the same, some -ar verbs change their spelling only in «yo». Verbs ending in «-car» become «-qué» («buscar → busqué»), those in «-gar» become «-gué» («llegar → llegué»), and those in «-zar» become «-cé» («empezar → empecé»). STEP 6: when the stem ends in a vowel, the «i» between two vowels becomes «y» in the third person: «leer → leyó, leyeron». The other forms carry an accent on the «í»: «leí, leíste, leímos, leísteis». «Creer» (creyó) and «oír» (oyó) do the same thing. STEP 7: «salir» is irregular only in the present («salgo»); in the indefinido it's regular: «salí, saliste, salió». STEP 8: a few very common verbs (ser, ir, hacer, tener, decir, ver) are irregular in the indefinido. Those are saved for lesson 20.
o português usa «-eu» na terceira pessoa: English past-tense verbs don't change their ending based on whether the root ends in a vowel or consonant, so the «i → y» spelling shift in «leyó», «creyó», «oyó» has no parallel to lean on — it's simply a Spanish spelling rule to learn on its own. The «-car/-gar/-zar» spelling changes (busqué, llegué, empecé) are the same kind of thing: a pattern that keeps the consonant sound stable in writing, with nothing in English's own spelling system to map it onto.

Indefinido ou perfecto, e três falsos am: Indefinido or perfecto, and three false friends
PASSO 1: pense no relógio. Se o período: STEP 1: think of the clock. If the period has already ended («ayer», «el lunes», «en 2019», «la semana pasada», «hace dos días»), use the indefinido: «Ayer compré pan» (yesterday I bought bread). STEP 2: if the period hasn't ended yet («hoy», «esta mañana», «esta semana», «este año»), Spain uses the pretérito perfecto: «Esta semana he trabajado mucho». STEP 3: in Latin America, the indefinido often takes the perfecto's place: «Esta semana trabajé mucho». Both versions are correct, each in its own region; pick one and stay consistent. STEP 4: to say «two days ago» about a past fact, put «hace» before the amount of time and nothing else: «Llegué hace dos días». You never say «hace dos días atrás». STEP 5: three false friends for talking about the past. «Cenar» and «la cena» mean «to have dinner» and «dinner» (the meal): «Cené a las ocho». «Un rato» means «a little while», not the rodent; the rodent is «ratón» (and «rata» is the bigger rat): «Esperé un rato» (I waited a little while). «Oficina» means «office» (the workplace): «Trabajé en la oficina».
o português do Brasil usa o mesmo pretér: English makes no distinction at all between «I ate yesterday» and «I've eaten today» in terms of which past tense to reach for — the simple past covers the first and the present perfect the second, but nothing about English grammar maps directly onto the Spain/Latin-America split here. Spain keeps «Ayer comí» (indefinido) and «Hoy he comido» (perfecto) strictly separate by whether the time period is closed or still open; in Latin America that line is looser, and the indefinido covers both cases.
